summary.text: A space station is a spacecraft that remains in orbit and hosts humans for extended periods, making it an artificial satellite with habitation facilities.
Most often stations have been research stations, but they have also served military or commercial uses, such as hosting space tourists.
The first was Salyut 1 in 1971, and today the International Space Station and China's Tiangong Space Station are the two fully operational ones.

paragraphs.heading: What a space station is
paragraphs.text: A space station is a spacecraft that stays in orbit and gives people a place to live for long stretches of time. Put another way, it is an artificial satellite with living quarters on board. Stations are often built from separate pieces called modules, joined at docking ports. Those ports let modules be added or moved, and they let visiting spacecraft drop off people, supplies and tools. Stations generally keep to the same orbit, but they still carry thrusters for station keeping.

paragraphs.heading: What stations are for
paragraphs.text: What a station is used for depends on the program that runs it. Most have been research stations, though some have had military jobs and others commercial ones, such as hosting space tourists. Each crew member usually spends weeks or months aboard, and rarely more than a year. Stations are the only places where people have kept up a continuous presence in space.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas on paper
paragraphs.text: Something like a space station first turned up in Edward Everett Hale's 1869 "The Brick Moon". Konstantin Tsiolkovsky and Hermann Oberth, about twenty years apart in the early 20th century, were the first to treat the idea seriously and scientifically. In 1929 Herman Potočnik pictured a station shaped like a rotating wheel, turning to create artificial gravity. Wernher von Braun published his own wheel design in Collier's Weekly in 1951, drawing on Potočnik. Still, nobody began building a rotating station during the 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Learning to meet in orbit
paragraphs.text: The Gemini program paved the way for stations. In 1965 Gemini 6 and Gemini 7 made the first meeting of two craft in space, without joining up. In 1966 Neil Armstrong flew the first docking ever on Gemini 8, and in 1967 Kosmos 186 and Kosmos 188 became the first spacecraft to dock automatically. In January 1969 Soyuz 4 and Soyuz 5 swapped crew while docked, though not through an inside passage, and in March Apollo 9 moved astronauts between two docked ships through the inside for the first time.

paragraphs.heading: The first stations
paragraphs.text: The Soviet Union launched the first station, Salyut 1, on April 19, 1971, and its first crew flew on the ill-fated Soyuz 11. Early stations were single pieces, built and launched whole, usually with all their supplies and research equipment already inside. A crew then flew up to join the station and do research. Once the supplies were used up, the station was abandoned. The early Soviet stations were all called Salyut, but they came in civilian and military types, and the military ones, Salyut 2, 3 and 5, were also known as Almaz.

paragraphs.heading: A second docking port
paragraphs.text: Salyut 6 and Salyut 7 each had two docking ports, so a second crew could visit, arriving in a new spacecraft. A Soyuz ferry could last 90 days in space before it had to be swapped for a fresh one, and this let crews keep the station staffed all the time. The extra port also let Progress supply vehicles dock, bringing fresh supplies for long missions. America's Skylab, in orbit from 1973 to 1979, also had two ports, but its extra one was never used. Shortly before Salyut 7 was abandoned, it hard docked with a TKS tug, proving the idea of stations built from modules.

paragraphs.heading: From Mir to today
paragraphs.text: Stations have run one after another since Skylab in 1973, and they have been occupied since 1987, starting with Mir. The handover from Mir to the International Space Station, or ISS, which took its first crew in 2000, has kept people in orbit without a break. Today two stations are fully working: the ISS, home to crews since Expedition 1 arrived in October 2000, and China's Tiangong, occupied since Shenzhou 14 in June 2022. The most people ever on one station at once is 13, first reached on the ISS in 2009. On May 30, 2023, the two stations together held 17 people, 11 on the ISS and 6 on Tiangong.
